title: Accounting as a Business Language
objective: Use accounting as a shared language across a business.
grammarDetail: Present perfect for ongoing results. Example: We have taught the sales team one definition of margin. They have used it consistently for a year.
grammarDeepDive: The present perfect is used in business English to connect a past action with a present result. At Czarnikow, you might say 'We have taught the sales team one definition of margin' — meaning the teaching happened in the past, but the result is still true now. This is one of the most important tenses in accounting language, because accounting is full of ongoing results: a policy that has been applied since January, a reconciliation that has been completed , a team that has used the same method for a year. title: Applying Accounting Principles in Practice
grammar: Modal verbs of obligation in formal writing
objective: Apply accuracy, consistency and transparency to real entries.
grammarDetail: Modal verbs of obligation.  Must, should, have to in formal writing. Example: Every grey area must be documented. Decisions should be consistent across periods.
grammarDeepDive: In business English, must , should and have to express different levels of obligation. Must is the strongest — it means there is no choice. Should is a recommendation — it means 'this is the best practice'. Have to expresses external obligation — it means 'the rules require it'. At Czarnikow, accounting principles use all three: Every grey area must be documented , Decisions should be consistent , The team has to follow the rule once it is written down . Both Oxford Practice Grammar (Eastwood) and English Grammar in Use (Murphy) agree that in formal business writing, must is preferred for internal policies and professional standards, while have to is more common for external regulations.
